question: to the Commission Arkadiusz Mularczyk (ECR) Subject:
German humanitarian payments to Polish victims of Nazi crimes – political decision pending by 17 June 2026

An open letter of 18 May 2026, signed by Poland’s main victim associations and the board of the Foundation for Polish-German Reconciliation1, calls for a German political decision by 17 June 2026 – the 35th anniversary of the conclusion of the Polish-German Treaty of Good Neighbourliness – to resume humanitarian payments to Polish victims of Nazi German crimes, with disbursements commencing in July 2026. Payments ceased in 2006. Fewer than 50 000 eligible survivors remain in Poland and this number is declining by approximately 800 per month. On 28 April 2026, Germany’s Ambassador to Poland, Miguel Berger, confirmed that the pending decision is purely political, not legal or operational2. The Joint Declaration of the Polish-German Intergovernmental Consultations of 1 December 2025 records Germany’s commitment to examine possibilities of providing additional support to Polish victims. Germany already applies humanitarian mechanisms to other surviving Nazi victim groups. 1.
Will the Commission use its stated facilitation role to encourage Germany to honour its commitment of 1 December 2025, given that its Ambassador has confirmed that no legal obstacle exists?
Does the exclusion of Polish victims from mechanisms applied to other Nazi victim groups comply with Article 21 of the Charter of Fundamental Rights of the European Union?
With 800 victims dying monthly, does the Commission consider a further delay to be compatible with the right to effective remedy under Directive 2012/29/EU?

answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (16.9.2026) Questions concerning the consequences of historical events, including reparations or compensation between Member States, are primarily the responsibility of the Member States concerned and fall outside the competences conferred upon the Commission by the EU Treaties1. Within the limits of its competences, the Commission remains firmly committed to support preserving the memory of the victims of the Second World War, promoting reconciliation, and fostering historical remembrance, dialogue and mutual understanding across the EU, in particular through relevant programmes such as the call on remembrance under the Citizens, Equality, Rights and Values (CERV) programme2. According to Article 51(1) of the EU Charter of Fundamental Rights3, the Charter is applicable to Members States only when they are implementing EU law. As regards specifically the access to reparation of Polish World War II victims and their families for harm caused during the war, there are no applicable EU rules on this matter. The Commission also recalls its replies to written parliamentary questions P-000819/20254 and P-002838/20245.
